segments.visual: Five clinic trays fade in. Chips pop in as hollow rings, then some fill. The question appears on top.

sentences.text: Here's a question that sounds simple.
Five clinics send their patients home. Some of those patients are back in hospital within thirty days. Which clinic is doing the best job?

segments.visual: Legend: filled chip = readmitted, hollow chip = not readmitted.

sentences.text: Each chip is one patient. A filled chip is a patient who was readmitted.

segments.visual: A rate bar and a percentage grow under each tray in turn.

sentences.text: The obvious move is to count. At Alder, 13 of 30 patients came back: that's 43%.
sentences.say: The obvious move is to count. At Alder, thirteen of thirty patients came back: that's forty-three percent.

sentences.text: Birch, 47%. Cedar, 40%. Dune, 58%. And at Elm, nobody at all.
sentences.say: Birch, forty-seven percent. Cedar, forty. Dune, fifty-eight. And at Elm, nobody at all.

segments.visual: The trays slide into rank order: Elm, Cedar, Alder, Birch, Dune. Rank numbers appear.

sentences.text: Line them up from lowest to highest, and we have a league table.
Elm in first place, Dune in last, and Alder just ahead of Birch.

segments.visual: Everything dims except Alder and Birch; a swap mark hangs between them.

sentences.text: It looks like an answer. But for those two, the table has it backwards.

segments.visual: Series logo and wordmark; arc and episode title.

sentences.text: Welcome to Model in Motion, where we build statistical models one moving piece at a time.
This is the start of a new story: how to compare providers fairly. Today, unfair comparisons, and what a fair one would need.

segments.visual: Alder and Birch as two large trays of jumbled chips.

sentences.text: Let's look more closely at Alder and Birch.
So far, we've treated every patient as interchangeable. They aren't.

segments.visual: A pale ring grows around every higher-risk patient.

sentences.text: Some are frail, or going home after a long and complicated stay. Patients like that are more likely to come back, wherever they're treated.
Let's mark those higher-risk patients with a ring.

segments.visual: Chips sort inside each tray: lower-risk left, higher-risk right.

sentences.text: Now sort the chips: lower-risk patients on the left, higher-risk on the right.

segments.visual: Counts appear under each pile; Alder's big lower-risk pile and Birch's big higher-risk pile light up.

sentences.text: Look at who each clinic is caring for. At Alder, 24 of the 30 patients are lower-risk.
sentences.say: Look at who each clinic is caring for. At Alder, twenty-four of the thirty patients are lower-risk.

sentences.text: Birch is the mirror image: 24 of its 30 are higher-risk.
sentences.say: Birch is the mirror image: twenty-four of its thirty are higher-risk.

segments.visual: The term 'case mix' appears.

sentences.text: This is a clinic's case mix: the kind of patients it serves. And these two could hardly be more different.

segments.visual: The higher-risk piles dim.

sentences.text: So let's compare like with like, starting with the lower-risk patients.

segments.visual: Row one of a scoreboard: 8 of 24 = 33% against 1 of 6 = 17%; Birch's number turns green.

sentences.text: At Alder, 8 of 24 were readmitted: one in three. At Birch, 1 of 6: about 17%.
sentences.say: At Alder, eight of twenty-four were readmitted: one in three. At Birch, one of six: about seventeen percent.

sentences.text: For these patients, Birch does better.

segments.visual: Row two: 5 of 6 = 83% against 13 of 24 = 54%; Birch's number turns green.

sentences.text: Now the higher-risk patients. Alder: 5 of 6, or 83%. Birch: 13 of 24, or 54%.
sentences.say: Now the higher-risk patients. Alder: five of six, or eighty-three percent. Birch: thirteen of twenty-four, or fifty-four percent.

sentences.text: Birch does better again.

segments.visual: Row three, everyone: 43% against 47%; this time Alder's number is the lower one.

sentences.text: Lower-risk patients do better at Birch. Higher-risk patients do better at Birch.
And yet, put everyone back together, and it's Alder with the lower rate.

segments.visual: The label 'Simpson's paradox' appears under the scoreboard.

sentences.text: Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic. This is Simpson's paradox, and it lies in wait wherever groups with different mixes are compared.

segments.visual: Two beams marked 0 to 100%. Each clinic's chips fly from its tray onto its beam, as a pile at each group's rate.

sentences.text: Here's what's going on. Give each clinic a beam, marked from zero to one hundred percent.
Each group of patients sits on the beam at its own readmission rate.

segments.visual: A pivot appears under Alder's beam; the beam tips toward the heavy pile.

sentences.text: A clinic's overall rate is the point where its beam balances. And that depends on how much weight sits at each end.

segments.visual: Alder's pivot slides left until the beam levels at 43%.

sentences.text: Alder's patients are mostly lower-risk, so its balance point sits near the low end: 43%.
sentences.say: Alder's patients are mostly lower-risk, so its balance point sits near the low end: forty-three percent.

segments.visual: Guides show both of Birch's piles left of Alder's. Birch's pivot slides right to 47%.

sentences.text: Birch's piles both sit further left: lower rates in both groups.
But most of its weight is at the higher-risk end, and that drags the balance point up to 47%.
sentences.say: But most of its weight is at the higher-risk end, and that drags the balance point up to forty-seven percent.

segments.visual: Two tags: where the piles sit = performance; how heavy they are = case mix.

sentences.text: So a raw rate blends two things: how well a clinic performs, and who walked in the door.

segments.visual: The chips trade beams: Birch's blue piles rise to Alder's beam, Alder's orange piles drop to Birch's.

sentences.text: Here's a way to feel the difference. Imagine the two clinics traded patients.

segments.visual: Alder's beam tips right; its pivot slides to 73%. A link joins it to Birch's own 47%.

sentences.text: Alder's two rates stay where they were. But now it carries Birch's patients, and its balance point slides all the way up to 73%.
sentences.say: Alder's two rates stay where they were. But now it carries Birch's patients, and its balance point slides all the way up to seventy-three percent.

sentences.text: With those same patients, Birch managed 47%.
sentences.say: With those same patients, Birch managed forty-seven.

segments.visual: Birch's pivot slides down to 24%. A second link joins it to Alder's own 43%.

sentences.text: And Birch, with Alder's easier mix? Its balance point falls to 24%, where Alder had 43%.
sentences.say: And Birch, with Alder's easier mix? Its balance point falls to twenty-four percent, where Alder had forty-three.

segments.visual: Both links lean the same way: on the same patients, Birch is lower both times.

sentences.text: Whichever set of patients you choose, Birch comes out well ahead. The league table had these two the wrong way round.

segments.visual: 200 dots appear as a block.

sentences.text: Two clinics could be a fluke. So let's zoom out to 200 providers.
sentences.say: Two clinics could be a fluke. So let's zoom out to two hundred providers.

sentences.text: They're simulated, which means we know how good each one truly is.

segments.visual: Dots line up along the bottom by true performance, then rise to their raw-rate rank.

sentences.text: Line them up from truly best on the left to truly worst on the right.
Then lift each one by its raw rate: lowest at the bottom, highest at the top.

segments.visual: A dashed diagonal; the readout shows rank correlation 0.16.

sentences.text: If raw rates told the truth, the dots would hug the diagonal. Instead, they're scattered almost everywhere: a rank correlation of just 0.16.
sentences.say: If raw rates told the truth, the dots would hug the diagonal. Instead, they're scattered almost everywhere: a rank correlation of just zero point one six.

segments.visual: A five-by-five grid; the diagonal blocks glow; dots outside them turn coral; 142 of 200.

sentences.text: Cut the table into fifths, and 142 of the 200 providers land in the wrong one.
sentences.say: Cut the table into fifths, and a hundred and forty-two of the two hundred providers land in the wrong one.

segments.visual: The x-axis is relabelled by how sick the patients are; dots slide sideways into a clear trend; 0.58.

sentences.text: Now re-sort the very same providers by how sick their patients are.
There's the pattern the raw rates were following all along: a correlation of 0.58.
sentences.say: There's the pattern the raw rates were following all along: a correlation of zero point five eight.

segments.visual: The league table returns; Elm and Dune light up.

sentences.text: There's a second problem in that league table, and it has nothing to do with case mix. Look at the two extremes.

segments.visual: The patient counts under Dune and Elm pulse: 12 and 11.

sentences.text: Dune's 58% rests on 12 patients. Elm's perfect zero, on 11.
sentences.say: Dune's fifty-eight percent rests on twelve patients. Elm's perfect zero, on eleven.

segments.visual: Outcomes are re-dealt again and again; bars jump; a tick is left at every rate visited.

sentences.text: So try an experiment. Suppose all five clinics were secretly identical: every patient with the same four-in-ten chance of coming back. Now deal out the luck. And again. And again.
Even the bigger clinics wobble. The smallest swing much further.

segments.visual: A bracket spans each clinic's ticks.

sentences.text: So before trusting any gap between providers, we'll have to ask how much of it chance alone could produce. That question gets an episode of its own.

segments.visual: Three recap cards, each with a small icon.

sentences.text: Let's gather it up.
A raw rate blends performance with case mix.
Compare like with like, and a ranking can flip.
And small providers swing with chance.

segments.visual: One chip sprouts many attribute tags; the two piles keep splitting into ever smaller ones.

sentences.text: What we really want is to compare providers as if they had all treated the same patients.
With one risk factor, sorting chips into two piles was enough. But real patients differ in dozens of ways at once.

segments.visual: The tags collapse onto one ruler from 0 to 100%; the chip slides along it. Next episode title.

sentences.text: So next time, we'll build a single ruler for risk: a way to turn everything we know about a patient into one probability.

segments.visual: Series end card with the next episode title.

sentences.text: This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
